lead.headline: Healey Delivers His First Budget With Little Room to Spend
lead.deck: A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is expected, with help on energy bills and a fuel duty freeze.
body: A Budget is the Chancellor's statement of how the government will raise and spend money. Chancellor John Healey, 101 days into the job, presents his first on 28 October to the House of Commons. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the official forecaster, publishes its economic and fiscal forecast the same day.

The mood music is steady rather than dramatic. Headtopics reports the Budget is meant to give 'breathing space' to hard-pressed households. Expected measures include energy bills support for poorer households, a freeze on fuel duty, action to help first-time buyers and tax relief for smaller businesses. To pay for some of it, Healey plans a new raid on banks and a crackdown on online retailers such as Amazon, eBay and Temu. The personal allowance, frozen at 12,570 pounds since 2022, is not expected to change in any major way.

The limit is money. Higher government borrowing costs linked to the Iran war have reduced Healey's room for manoeuvre. The OBR forecast a buffer of about 24 billion pounds in March; the Resolution Foundation estimates it has roughly halved to 12 billion pounds. A new tax allowance is planned for low-income pensioners who would otherwise be pulled into the tax system for the first time, though experts have called the proposal 'messy' and warned of 'cliff edges'.

Healey has said the Budget will move money and power out of Westminster and into every postcode around Britain, and that it will meet the government's fiscal rules, the self-imposed limits on borrowing.

world.headline: Three-Way Ukraine Talks Are Set for Next Month, Without a Pause in Fighting
world.deck: For Europe, the talks decide a security question on its own doorstep.
body: Ukraine, Russia and the United States have agreed to hold three-way talks next month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 26 October. The Kremlin has since said it agreed in principle to a meeting on 10 November in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. Europe is not named as a party in this report, even though the war is on the European continent.

Russia's President Vladimir Putin said on 23 October that renewed talks must focus on security for Russia, Ukraine and Europe overall, according to The Moscow Times. That wording matters to European governments, because it puts Europe's own security on the agenda.

But there is no truce attached. Russia has said it has no intention of halting hostilities during the talks, Ukrainska Pravda reported, and Putin has said he wants final agreements rather than a short-lived ceasefire. Zelenskyy, for his part, has renewed his call for a meeting with Putin on territorial issues.

Europe's own part is harder to pin down. On 20 October Zelenskyy met US envoy Steve Witkoff and European leaders in Oslo. Witkoff then carried new ideas, worked out with European countries and Ukraine, to Russia. The Kremlin brushed them aside: Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov said there wasn't really much substance in them.

On 27 October the leaders of Finland and Norway held a rare direct call with Putin, which the Finnish president's office said was arranged from Helsinki. Moscow played the call down and blamed EU and NATO policies for dragging out the war. Not every European capital welcomed it: Denmark's Prime Minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she was very sceptical about reaching out to Putin and urged Europe to act together.

The hardest question is still land. Russia demands that Ukraine leave the part of the eastern Donetsk region it still holds, and Ukraine says that would amount to surrender. Whether the 10 November date holds, and who will speak for Europe, are the next things to watch.

uk.headline: UK Inflation Climbs to 3.5% as Fuel Costs Rise
uk.deck: The figure for September lands a week before the Budget.
body: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise over a year. In September UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5%, up from 3.1% in August, driven mainly by fuel, according to the figures reported by ITV News.

Motor fuels cost 30% more than a year earlier, up from a 23% rise in August. Average petrol reached 169.5p a litre, the highest in around four years, and diesel hit 192.5p, its highest since July 2022. Reports attribute the rise to the Iran war, which has squeezed global oil and gas supplies.
Some economists think the rise could prompt the Bank of England to raise interest rates next month.

The rise is not only about fuel. Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, went up from 2.6% to 2.8%, and inflation in services rose from 3.4% to 3.7%, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

Chancellor John Healey blamed the price rises on conflicts in the Middle East and Europe. The Bank of England's next interest-rate decision is on 5 November, and the ONS publishes October's inflation figures on 18 November.
uk.why: Fuel is a cost for nearly every journey and delivery, so a big rise at the pump can lift prices in shops as well.
also: Fuel duty: The Budget is expected to freeze fuel duty, according to Headtopics.
Pensions: A new allowance for low-income pensioners is planned, with experts warning of 'cliff edges'.

europe.headline: Europe's Cost-of-Living Anger Spills Into the Streets
europe.deck: Protests in France, Italy and Portugal follow sharp rises in fuel and energy bills.
body: Across Europe, higher fuel and energy bills have set off protests. In France, weekend unrest led to 2,400 arrests, France 24 reports; President Emmanuel Macron said the protesters' demands were legitimate while condemning violence and looting. In Milan, police clashed with protesters over poor public services and rising living costs, and thousands marched in Portugal against housing costs, according to CNBC.

The numbers are large. The European Commission estimates the Iran conflict has cost Europe roughly 100 billion euros through disrupted trade and energy markets. Gas prices have jumped about 140% and diesel prices have doubled. In France, energy prices rose 21.3% year on year in September, according to the statistics office INSEE.

Politics is shifting too. In Germany, the AfD is pushing to restore energy ties with Russia, and in Poland energy-bill concerns are helping the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown, France 24 reports.

lead.headline: The UK Budget Is Due on 28 October
body: John Healey is the UK's Chancellor. He will present his first Budget on 28 October. A Budget is a plan for taxes and spending.
He is expected to help poorer homes with energy bills and to freeze fuel duty. He also plans to take more money from banks.
There is not much spare money. A cushion of 24 billion pounds was forecast in March. It may now be about 12 billion pounds.

world.headline: Ukraine, Russia and the US Plan Talks
body: Ukraine's president says Ukraine, Russia and the US will hold talks next month. Russia says they could meet on 10 November in Abu Dhabi.
Russia's president, Vladimir Putin, says talks must cover security for Europe too.
Russia also says it will not stop fighting during the talks. Putin says he wants lasting peace deals, not a short pause. Ukraine's president also wants to meet Putin to talk about land.

uk.headline: UK Prices Rise Faster
body: Prices in the UK rose 3.5% in a year to September. That is more than the 3.1% in August.
Fuel was the main reason. Motor fuels cost 30% more than a year before.
Petrol averaged 169.5p a litre, the highest in about four years. Diesel reached 192.5p a litre. Reports say the Iran war has squeezed oil and gas supplies.

europe.headline: People in Europe Protest Over Prices
body: Fuel and energy bills have risen across Europe. People have protested in France, Italy and Portugal.
In France, 2,400 people were arrested after weekend unrest. The EU's Commission says the Iran conflict has cost Europe about 100 billion euros.
Gas prices have jumped about 140%, and diesel prices have doubled. In Milan, police clashed with protesters. In Portugal, thousands marched against high housing costs.
